newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel security crisis hides deep Middle East gloom.
newsitem.headline: Israel security crisis hides deep Middle East gloom.

text.p: When two militant Islamic suicide bombers brought carnage to Jerusalem's main Jewish market last week, their action not only threw the focus of Middle East peacemaking firmly onto Israel's security.
It also widened an existing gulf of mutual mistrust between Israeli and Palestinian leaders which some analysts say has pushed prospects for a durable peace settlement years over the horizon.
"I think there will be continual talks. Talking is easy," said Professor Efraim Inbar, director of the Begin-Sadat Center for Strategic Studies in Tel Aviv.
"There will be pressure on the part of the Americans...but basically we see a moribund peace process. It's not a coffin yet, it's not dead but it's in serious trouble," he said.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Wednesday that she planned to go to the Middle East at the end of August provided envoy Dennis Ross, due at the weekend, could deliver progress on security in the wake of last week's attack.

Her aim will be to accelerate work on talks on the shape of a final peace settlement, a step she said would require "a clear, mutual and favourable sense of the ultimate direction of negotiation" by the two sides.

That sense is what analysts say is sorely lacking between Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, who accuse each other of violating interim accords for Palestinian self-rule.

They say the depth of recrimination, over Israeli settlement building on occupied Arab land and over Palestinian failure to crack down on militants, strikes at the foundation for future peace laid in the 1993 Oslo accords.

When Netanyahu answered last week's bombings with an economic and security clampdown on Palestinian areas to pressure Arafat into action against the militants, it only deepened Palestinian doubts about the right-wing leader's agenda.
"He is willing to dismantle and destroy these Oslo accords," said Ahmed Tibi, a senior adviser to Arafat.

He said Arafat remained ready to "do business" with Netanyahu but left little doubt that the Palestinian Authority saw scant hope of significant negotiated progress as long as the Likud party leader was in office.

"We are not waiting for the downfall of Mr Netanyahu because I am not expressing my dreams publicly," Tibi said, adding that Israelis had to choose between "Netanyahu's vision or the vision of cooperation, co-existence and peace".

This pessimism is mirrored on the Israeli side, where a willingness to regard Arafat as a reliable negotiating partner who has renounced violence was diminishing even before last week's 13 killings by the two as yet unidentified bombers.

"The whole process of implementing the Oslo agreements has been transformed from a confidence-building into a confidence-destroying measure," said Israeli analyst Mark Heller of the Jaffee Centre for Strategic Studies.
"What the crushing majority of the Israeli public wants or expects out of this process is simply more personal security. That confidence is eroding," he said.

The "core bargain" of Israel's interim peace deals with Arafat, inherited by Netanyahu with distaste from previous Labour governments, was that Israel would get "peace" while the Palestinians would get "land".

Even before the bombings, confidence-building aspects of those accords, such as opening air and sea ports in Palestinian self-ruled Gaza, had already been on hold because of Israel's expansion of Jewish settlements.

Palestinians regard the construction as a strategy by Netanyahu to pre-empt the outcome on the crucial issues of final peace talks, including the extent of a Palestinian homeland and the status of Arab East Jerusalem.
Israel in turn considers Arafat to have taken the view that violence has now become an option in trying to achieve his Palestinian state.

One senior Israeli official, who is by no means a hawk, said the entire peace process was in "deep, solid and continuous crisis" as a result of the absence of confidence and the depth of disagreement over final status issues.

"The most positive result we can get in the coming years is a co-existence with cooperation in security and other matters while understanding that there are issues that can't be agreed," said the official.
"The other possibility is more and more friction, low intensity conflict for a long time between the two sides."
